notEstablished.revitalisation: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act, Cap. 86, was read end to end: it names language only in its statement of goals, at goal (g) on knowledge and understanding of the history, language, culture, rights and values of Grenadians, and in its offence and teacher-qualification sections, and it sets up no body, programme or funding for any language. SUMMA's Grenada country review records one language activity, a local programme called Spice Signs teaching sign language on the Government Information Station daily since the onset of COVID-19, which it frames as support for children with special needs rather than as reversing language shift; it records nothing on a Grenadian vernacular.

Not established from the sources consulted. The Ministry of Education's own Reimagining Education in Barbados reform paper proposes only functional foreign languages as a curricular addition and names no promotion, academy or programme for the local vernacular. The Education Act, Cap. 41 (L.R.O. 1997, as amended) uses the word language only three times, each of them in an offence provision about insulting, abusive or indecent language to a teacher or school attendance officer, and carries no language-of-education or language-promotion clause at all.

Not established from the sources consulted. Ley 66-97, Ley General de Educación, names lengua only in generic curricular aims - expression in the lengua materna, the basics of at least one lengua extranjera, the value of a command of lenguas - and establishes no body, programme or funding to promote any named language. Ley 139-01 on higher education, science and technology contains no occurrence of lengua or idioma at all. The UNESCO PEER profile cited on this entry can no longer be read: education-profiles.org now serves only an archive notice pointing to the new PEER site, which has no Dominican Republic page at the paths tried.

Not established from the sources consulted. The Landsverordening officiële talen was read in full, all eight articles: it fixes English and Dutch as the official languages, governs which of them the government uses with residents, and empowers rules on their spelling, but sets out no promotion, revival or maintenance measure and names no other language. The Ministry's 2022 Sint Maarten Education Review discusses language only as a medium-of-instruction and pupil-proficiency problem, recommending that schools develop language policies that take account of pupils' varying native languages; it names no revitalisation activity, actor or funding.
